Recently, I've been doing job interviews. Among the classic range of "type" questions and answers in these kinds of encounters, I was asked a question that I particularly enjoy remembering. They asked why I chose computer science; what paths led me to do what I do. I remember looking up, thinking for a few seconds, and starting my answer by saying, "Now that I think about it, the truth is it's a good story...".

I got into computers when I was young, drawn in by video games. At that time, my older sister's boyfriend used to come over a lot and talk to me about computers. I have to thank my grandfather for the effort of buying a 386 PC with a few megabytes of RAM, on which I played "Prince of Persia" and "The Secret of Monkey Island". Soon, I got tired of video games and started to be interested in the architecture and structure of the computer, which inevitably led to several formats, reboots, and various setups. My mother always said we would all end up electrocuted.

Things wouldn't have gone further if it hadn't been for a high school teacher (back then it was seventh grade in EGB) who greatly influenced me at that tender age. I don’t know if it’s common among teenagers, but in my case, I was looking for role models, roles, and mentors. I’m afraid I found it in him, whether he liked it or not.

This teacher had a place inherited in the neighborhood of the school that he used to correct exams, so he didn't have to work at home. On the first floor, he had two computers (the good and the bad), a pool table, and an extensive library. One of the most beautiful and charming ones I remember. On the ground floor, he had a foosball table (a downfall for any teenager) and a small rehearsal space where a band of his acquaintances played. That's how I grew up during those tender years—between keyboards and computers, foosball games, books, and live music. What more could you ask for? I remember reading classics like Macbeth and dabbling with the now obsolete Corel Draw.

Because he was a teacher, he had some special condition for contracting internet, some improvements in the rates, I think. In those days, you paid per use with a 56kb modem. Since there were many of us who wanted to enjoy the virtues of that fledgling internet and stop looking at the computer as a dumb, static box and start seeing it as a window to the world, we had to come up with a system to pay the bills together. This was the key to my education because the environment in that place was very technological and academic, the average age was much higher than mine, and in those few square meters, I saw real experts in many fields. Since there were no obligations and everything was done from a leisure perspective, anyone who wanted to take an interest in something was welcome, and anyone who didn't could always go downstairs to play foosball. Gradually, I wanted to get into the world of Linux and programming. I wore out my poor 386 (Lucy, I called it then, in honor of the Beatles song: "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds") with programs made in BASIC with horrible syntax and limited functionality.

One of the older guys was studying the beginning of the computer science degree, which, if I’m not mistaken, at that time was only offered by the Autonomous University of Barcelona under the name "Bachelor of Science" (in capital letters). He came up with a very simple idea to make a "taximeter" type program that would count the minutes each person connected to the internet, convert it to pesetas (the old Spanish currency), and fill a piggy bank to pay the bill at the end of the month.

That simple idea turned into a pretty well-made Visual Basic program that was expanded with users, profiles, and everything we could think of to improve it. It was then that three of us who frequented the place became interested in it and asked him to give us a Visual Basic course. The course didn’t last long, but it was one of my first forays into the field.

Like any good teenager, I was incapable of focusing on just one thing and insisted on devouring philosophy, theater, novels, and essays; listening to recommended albums and memorizing hundreds of songs; and also wanted to get into art! One of my schoolmates had (and still has) a wonderful talent for drawing and everything related to illustration. He always told me he made comics at home and showed me things, but never quite defined a long project. My talent with a pencil is more than zero, but I’ve always been very enthusiastic about inventing stories and telling tales. So, we formed a writer and artist duo and started making comics with a beginning, middle, and end. Since the protagonists of our stories were our friends and acquaintances, it was very popular among those around us. Soon, due to the technological environment of the place, the idea of making a website about our comic projects quickly emerged. So, at fourteen, I wrote my first website in rudimentary and terrible HTML.

The nice thing is that I still keep in touch with some of those childhood friends, fifteen years later, and the funniest thing is that that primitive, stone-age website... still exists! Today, I found it by chance and the time travel was dizzying. It gave me a strange feeling in my stomach, flashes passing before my eyes, a taste in my mouth of lemon ice pops and sunflower seeds. I remembered melodies of songs we sang at the top of our lungs with the inner peace of those who have no inkling of what's coming their way. I recalled movie tickets for six hundred pesetas, with a bag of candies and stolen kisses in doorways. We were creative, imaginative, had initiative, enthusiasm, drive, and hope. Above all, hope. Hope to escape an unfair neighborhood with very harsh and strict laws, hope to honor our parents and fulfill their dream of finally having what they couldn't. To jump fences, dodge bullets, and only look back to say goodbye to those who stayed behind, fleeing forward.

That’s why I do what I do today, even though I had no idea those years would define much of my adult life. At fifteen, all you want is to have fun and create great friendships, the kind that burn a bit inside and leave a scar that hurts when the weather changes and it looks like rain.

It's funny how details can end up defining the whole. Those two or three right decisions at the right time have led me to be what I am and do what I do. So, the answer to the question should have been... "Actually, it was all a series of circumstances, three-cushion billiard caroms I was trying to master on the first floor, having ice cream with this person and not that one. For all those summed-up reasons, we’re here today, talking about my professional life." Instead, I gave some bland, textbook, well-formed, and convincing answer that got me the ultimate goal of passing the interview successfully. It would have been much better to go for a drink in a relaxed setting, tell him my story, and hear his. Now, reflecting on that moment, I realize I’m left wanting to know his story.
